cautions: EVERY calculation published in this subject must be executed with Bash (python3) before it ships — the worked example, any number in the prose, and any arithmetic inside a question or its explanation. State units at every step and carry them through. A wrong worked example is the worst failure mode in a technical subject because students check their work against it.
Use SI units as primary. Where U.S. customary units are conventional in American practice, give both and show the conversion with the NIST-defined factor.
Significant figures and precision must be handled honestly: do not report more digits than the inputs justify, and say so when rounding.

Engineering standards (ASME, ASTM, IEEE, ISO, ACI, AISC) are copyrighted and mostly paywalled. Describe what a standard governs and cite it by designation, but never reproduce standard text, tables, or values — and never state a specific allowable stress, load factor, or design value as if from a standard you did not read.

This subject is safety-adjacent. Teach principles, never design guidance a reader could apply to a real structure, pressure vessel, electrical installation, or machine. Add an explicit statement that lessons are educational material and not engineering design guidance, and that real design requires a licensed engineer working to the governing code.

Distinguish idealized models from reality throughout — rigid bodies, frictionless surfaces, ideal gases, ohmic conductors, and small-deflection assumptions all have limits, and naming those limits is part of the lesson.
Do not overstate factor-of-safety practice as universal; it varies by code, industry, and failure consequence.
